title: Tom Owens's Charlie Parker study and how improvisation works
summary: Patrick describes the Parker research on recurring melodic figures; Carter agrees improvisers reuse figures over chord structures.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Well, let me ... or maybe I could put it another way or refer to something.
All right, do.

I think it doesn't come as any surprise that there hasn't been very much ... what you might call serious musical research or serious analytical study about jazz by music scholars. However, in the last few years, this sounds bibliographical now, but nonetheless, but there has been a very important piece of work done on Charlie Parker -- now, this is your interview, but I'm just using this as an example.
Sure ... yes.

... by a fellow named Tom Owens, who worked about 10 years on this dissertation which, when it finally came in, was about 1,000 pages long - and half of it was a series of transcriptions of several hundred transcriptions

and the upshot of his research was that by looking at several hundred of these transcriptions of Parker, what he did was isolate 100 very short, melodic figures, which Parker would use over and over and over again, but in innumerable numbers of combinations.

And not randomly, by any means -- but, that each one of these little melodic figures, or motives, modals, whatever we care to call them, had a characteristic use, and so that in a certain sense, Parker's improvisations, perhaps we can put quotation marks around the word "improvisations" were a process by which he continually refashioned and strung all his these little figures together, although his music certainly doesn't sound like that at all, and this is perhaps a very different notion of what we normally think of as improvisation, if you look in to a dictionary, we're told that it's new, it's unique, it's original, it's simultaneously composed while it's being performed, etc.

But perhaps this being, as far as I know, the only really large scale study of at least a single jazz figure's technique of improvisation, suggests something about the mechanics of what improvising is.

Well, I think Parker would certainly, undoubtedly be the outstanding example, but I think this applies to almost any improvisation that I think you would hear coming out of a musician's instrument, and you would find this pattern

persisting, something that he would do according to the chord structure. You know, there'd be a figure or a number of different figures that he would use at a particular chord change, depending, you know, on the tempo and ...
The key and so on.

Yeah, the key and all of that. Yes, you know. Of course, I understand that this is not necessarily exclusive to jazz. It is maybe thought of now as being just a jazz thing -- jazz improvisation. But improvisation was not unknown to classical players, you know.
No, of course not.
... a couple of centuries ago, you know.
